lesson.menu_title: Handling Uncertainty with an Honest Answer
lesson.menu_desc: Modals of deduction -- must / might / cannot be -- plus ballpark figures and "I will get back to you" -- reading model -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 24 — Handling Uncertainty with an Honest Answer
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 24 — Handling Uncertainty with an Honest Answer
lesson.grammar_point: modals of deduction (must be / might be / cannot be)

listenings.text: I run a lot of meetings, and the question I fear the least is the one I cannot answer. That surprises people, so let me explain. When I do not know something, I give three things instead of one. First, what I do know. Off the top of my head, it is around forty. Second, how sure I am. That is an educated guess, not a promise, and it cannot be more than fifty because of the size of the team. Third, a deadline. I will double-check with finance and get back to you by four. Three sentences, and the meeting moves on. What kills a meeting is not I do not know. It is I do not know, said alone, with nothing after it. The room does not need certainty from you. It needs a number to work with and a time when the real one arrives.

English carries certainty in three small words, and once you hear them you cannot stop noticing them. Must, might, and cannot. If I say the client must be annoyed, I am not guessing wildly. I have a reason: they have written twice this week. Must is the strong one. If I say the client might be annoyed, I genuinely do not know, and I am opening a door rather than closing it. And if I say the client cannot be annoyed, I am almost as sure as with must, only in the opposite direction. Here is why this matters at work. People do not mind when you are unsure. They mind when they cannot tell how unsure you are. Put the right word in front of your guess and you have told them everything they need. One more thing: after these words the verb never changes. It is must be, might be, cannot be. Never must to be.

extra_audio.text: First, I say what I do know, straight away: off the top of my head, it is around forty. Then I add the reason behind it, so the number is not floating in the air. After that, I mark how sure I am: it must be close to that, and it cannot be more than fifty. Next, I name the limit of what I know, so nobody treats my guess as a fact. In the end, I promise a real deadline: I will double-check and get back to you by four.

reading.rtitle: Re: numbers for the Thursday board meeting
paras: Hi Daniel. Thanks for the heads-up. I do not have the exact figure in front of me, so please read the numbers below as a ballpark and not as the final answer.

Off the top of my head, we closed somewhere around forty accounts last quarter. It cannot be more than fifty, because we only had four people on the team until May. As far as I know, none of the June contracts have been signed yet, so presumably they will land in the next cycle.

The one number I would not guess is the churn rate. My educated guess is that it is under six percent, but that is exactly the kind of figure the board will check, so I would rather not put it on a slide today.
I am going to look into it this afternoon and double-check both numbers with finance. I will get back to you by four, and you will have the final version well before Thursday.
reading.source: Work email -- Vanessa to Daniel, Tuesday 09:12

gist.prompt: What is the main purpose of this email?
choices: To refuse to give any numbers before the board meeting
To give useful estimates now and promise the exact numbers by a deadline
To complain that the board meeting was moved to Thursday

items: The writer has the exact figures in front of her.
"I do not have the exact figure in front of me."
She is confident the number cannot be higher than fifty.
"It cannot be more than fifty, because we only had four people on the team until May."
She is happy to put the churn rate on a slide today.
"I would rather not put it on a slide today."
She commits to a specific time to come back with the numbers.
"I will get back to you by four."
